proposals.before: In 208 Cao Cao abolished the old Han ministerial posts, restored the chancellorship, and filled it himself, concentrating supreme executive power.
proposals.after: In the thirteenth year of Jian'an (208), the Han ministerial posts were abolished, the chancellorship was reinstated, and Lord Cao held it, thereby combining the highest civil authority.
proposals.reason: The Chinese makes the Han terrace ministers the object of abolition and 曹公 the holder of the restored chancellorship; the idiomatic version makes Cao Cao the agent of the abolition.

proposals.before: Hidden dragons and soaring swans, talents weighed like gold against jade—think of Baili Xi, of Zichan's picks, or Chu officers serving Jin: the tools of antiquity for finding ministers were plain enough.
proposals.after: Hidden dragons and soaring swans, talents weighed like gold against jade—Qin Xi, Zheng Chan, and Chu talent employed by Jin: these too were fine instruments of former times, and no less manifest.
proposals.reason: 秦奚 and 鄭產 are two named exemplars; 'Zichan's picks' invents a possessive and misses 鄭產 as the person named.

proposals.before: When the Three Corps followed, they swelled with crack troops like the ancient palace guard.
proposals.after: When the Three Departments were established, there were masses like those of Xiong Qu and Ci Fei.
proposals.reason: The idiomatic line drops the named exemplars 熊渠 and 佽飛, which the Chinese and the literal both preserve.

proposals.before: The cluster full headquarters, ritual parity with the Three Departments was Han in origin.
proposals.after: Opening a headquarters with ritual parity with the Three Excellencies was a Han office.
proposals.reason: Idiomatic English is ungrammatical and misrenders 開府儀同三司 as a confused cluster phrase.

proposals.before: Otherwise old rules held through three reigns until collapse.
proposals.after: The rest followed the old regulations through the three reigns of Wu, Hui, and Xiaohuai.
proposals.reason: The idiomatic line drops 武、惠、孝懷 and invents until collapse.

proposals.before: In 216 Xiahou Dun commanded twenty-six armies after the Wu campaign—a milestone.
proposals.after: In 216, returning from the campaign against Sun Quan, Xiahou Dun supervised twenty-six armies; this is an instance.
proposals.reason: Idiomatic English hides 孫權 as the Wu campaign and invents a milestone for 是也.

proposals.before: The Minister of Education added left and right chief clerks at one thousand shi;
proposals.after: The Minister over the Masses added left and right chief clerks at one thousand shi;
proposals.reason: 司徒 is Minister of Education here but Minister over the Masses in s0051.

proposals.before: 227 CE Sima Yi took the supreme commander title for the Shu expedition.
proposals.after: In the autumn of Emperor Ming of Wei's fourth Taihe year, Prince Xuan campaigned against Shu and added the title supreme commander.
proposals.reason: The idiomatic line fuses the year onto Sima Yi and omits 魏明帝, 秋, and source 宣帝.

proposals.before: Under Zhang of Later Han, Grand Tutor Zhao Xi and Minister of War Mou Rong both recorded Secretariat affairs.
proposals.after: Under Emperor Zhang of Later Han, Grand Tutor Zhao Xi and Minister of War Mou Rong both recorded Secretariat affairs.
proposals.reason: Idiomatic Zhang omits that 漢章帝 is Emperor Zhang; the clipped form is easily read as an unrelated personal name.

proposals.before: In the fourth year of Jiushi under Chengdi the Zhongshu eunuchs were abolished and five Masters of Writing were again appointed—one serving as vice director and four forming four bureaus jointly handling archives, secret records, and memorials, each with its charge.
proposals.after: In the fourth year of Jianshi under Chengdi the Zhongshu eunuchs were abolished and five Masters of Writing were again appointed—one serving as vice director and four forming four bureaus jointly handling archives, secret records, and memorials, each with its charge.
proposals.reason: 建始 is Jianshi, not Jiushi; the literal romanization invents a different era name.

proposals.before: When Wu founded the Secretariat in 29 BCE he attached four assistant commissioners.
proposals.after: When Emperor Wu of Han established the Secretariat in the fourth year of Jianshi, four assistants were immediately placed.
proposals.reason: The Chinese names 漢武帝 and 建始四年; idiomatic Wu plus a converted 29 BCE year hides the source era wording and the source emperor-era pairing.

proposals.before: chief clerk, merit clerk, household commander, recorder, armor office, gentlemen-thieves office, camp army, malfeasance clerk, household-area commander, merit clerk assistants, gate clerks, household clerks—one each.
proposals.after: registrar, merit clerk, household commander, recorder, armor-and-gentlemen-thieves offices, camp-army and malfeasance clerks, household-area commander, merit-clerk assistants and gate clerks, household clerks—one each.
proposals.reason: 主簿 is the registrar, not a second chief clerk; 長史 already occupies that sense in the preceding sentence.

proposals.before: 234 CE added Capital Officials and Cavalry bureaus for twenty-five lines.
proposals.after: In the second year of Qinglong, Minister Chen Jiao memorialized to add Capital Officials and Cavalry, making twenty-five gentlemen in all.
proposals.reason: The idiomatic English drops Qinglong and the named minister 陳矯, leaving only a Western year and bureau names.

proposals.before: Attendants traced to Feng Hou; Zhou called similar posts permanent stewards; Qin revived the title and Han kept it.
proposals.after: Palace attendants are traced to Feng Hou under the Yellow Emperor; under Zhou the duty matched the permanent steward; Qin borrowed the ancient name to establish palace attendants, and Han continued it.
proposals.reason: The idiomatic version omits 黃帝, to whom 風後 is attached as 侍中.

proposals.before: Wei fused freelance riders with standing attendants as feather-light counselors—fur pouch on the right, mounted escort—and Jin kept the mold.
proposals.after: At the start of Huangchu, Emperor Wen of Wei restored unattached cavalry and merged them with palace standing attendants to offer counsel without managing affairs; marten-fur bags were tucked on the right as they rode in loose escort—unchanged through Jin.
proposals.reason: The idiomatic English omits 魏文帝 and 黃初初.

proposals.before: 296 CE briefly saw the eunuch Dong Meng as standing attendant—then the experiment ended.
proposals.after: In Yuankang, Emperor Hui first made the eunuch Dong Meng a palace standing attendant; afterward the practice stopped.
proposals.reason: The idiomatic English replaces 元康中 and 惠帝 with a lone Western year.

proposals.before: Wu invented supernumerary deputies; 318 CE Yuan rotated two with regular deputies—'general-access' deputies—and later raised them to four.
proposals.after: Originally Emperor Wu established supernumerary elite cavalry deputy gentlemen; in the first year of Taixing, Emperor Yuan made two men rotate jointly with the elite cavalry deputy gentlemen—hence general-access elite cavalry deputy gentlemen—later increased to four.
proposals.reason: Bare 'Wu' and fused '318 CE Yuan' obscure 武帝 and 元帝 and drop 太興元年.

proposals.before: Later Han cashiered the Three Dukes and packed the audience rolls with kin and nobles.
proposals.after: In Eastern Han, many of the Three Dukes, imperial in-laws, imperial clansmen, and nobles held court-attending status.
proposals.reason: The Chinese lists 三公、外戚、宗室、諸侯 together as groups who 多奉朝請, not a cashiering of the Three Dukes alone.

proposals.before: Wudi named Miao Zheng Zhongshu compiler.
proposals.after: Wudi named Miao Zheng as Zhongshu compiler.
proposals.reason: The idiomatic English fuses the personal name Miao Zheng with the Zhongshu office, which invited a false person-name span.

proposals.before: 364 CE folded Coachman into Education.
proposals.after: 364 CE folded the Chamberlain for Attendants into the Minister of Education.
proposals.reason: Guanglu xun is the Chamberlain for Attendants, not the Coachman; situ is the Minister of Education.

proposals.before: In the second year of Xing'ning under Emperor Ai the Imperial Coachman was abolished and merged into the Minister of Education.
proposals.after: In the second year of Xing'ning under Emperor Ai the Chamberlain for Attendants was abolished and merged into the Minister of Education.
proposals.reason: The Chinese office abolished is Guanglu xun, not Taipu.

proposals.before: 373 CE revived the Coachman.
proposals.after: 373 CE revived the Chamberlain for Attendants.
proposals.reason: The restored office in the preceding sentence is Guanglu xun, not the Coachman.

proposals.before: Han titled empress-dowager suites above homonymous ministers; without a dowager the seats stayed empty.
proposals.after: The Three Ministers of the Empress Dowager—Commandant of the Guards, Privy Treasurer, and Minister Coachman—were established in Han; their titles followed the empress dowager's palace, ranking above ministers of the same name, and stayed vacant when there was no empress dowager.
proposals.reason: The idiomatic sentence drops the three Han offices (衛尉、少府、太僕), the Han founding, and palace-based title naming, collapsing them into an inaccurate 'suites' summary.

proposals.before: Han kept the pattern; in 7 BCE the censor-in-chief became Grand Minister of Works with a chief clerk, but the assistant director stayed unchanged.
proposals.after: Han followed this; in the first year of Suihe under Emperor Cheng (7 BCE) the Censor-in-Chief was renamed Grand Minister of Works and a chief clerk was established, while the assistant director's duties remained as before.
proposals.reason: The idiomatic rendering omits Emperor Cheng and the era name 綏和, leaving only a Western year.

proposals.before: Under Jin, nine posts were established at the same grade as document clerks, but they covered thirteen desks: Personnel, Merit Ranking, Duty Affairs, Seals, Inner Area Command, Outer Area Command, Matchmaking, Tallies, Water, Inner Rampart, Camp Army, Law, and Arithmetic.
proposals.after: Under Jin, nine posts were established at the same grade as the law-editing attendant censors, but they covered thirteen desks: Personnel, Merit Ranking, Duty Affairs, Seals, Inner Area Command, Outer Area Command, Matchmaking, Tallies, Water, Inner Rampart, Camp Army, Law, and Arithmetic.
proposals.reason: 品同治書 refers to the same grade as 治書侍御史 (law-editing attendant censors), not generic 'document clerks'.

proposals.before: As Prince of Jin he ran forces for the future emperor.
proposals.after: When the emperor was Prince of Jin, he entrusted him to manage military affairs.
proposals.reason: Idiomatic English invents a distinct future emperor; 帝為晉王 continues the emperor (文帝) as Prince of Jin commissioning Chen Xie.

proposals.before: After Shu's fall Chen Xie absorbed Zhuge Liang's formations and dual-camp signals—Wudi made him hall corps gentleman then general.
proposals.after: After Shu fell he ordered Xie to receive Zhuge Liang's encirclement formations and the hidden methods of maneuver and ambush, as well as the first-and-second camp banner system; Xie practiced them all to mastery and was therefore made palace hall gentleman commanding troops, later promoted general.
proposals.reason: English names Wudi as the appointer though the Chinese subject continues from 帝; 暗練 is mastery by practice, not a Wudi-specific invention.

proposals.before: After Shu fell he ordered Xie to receive Zhuge Liang's encirclement formations and maneuver secrets of troops and ambush, as well as the first-second camp banner systems—Xie mastered them all in darkness; therefore Xie was made palace hall gentleman commanding troops as gentleman-of-the-palace, later promoted general.
proposals.after: After Shu fell he ordered Xie to receive Zhuge Liang's encirclement formations and methods of troop maneuvers and ambush, as well as the A/B camp banner system; Xie practiced them all to fluency; therefore Xie was made palace hall gentleman-of-the-household commanding troops, later promoted general.
proposals.reason: 暗練 means practiced to fluency, not 'in darkness'; 中郎將 is duplicated as both gentleman commanding troops and gentleman-of-the-palace.

proposals.before: Under Jin, Colonel Directors, Colonel Protectors, Left and Right Guards, Valiant Cavalry, and Mobile Corps formed the Six Armies.
proposals.after: Under Jin, the Army Commander, Army Protector, Left and Right Guards, Valiant Cavalry, and Mobile Corps formed the Six Armies.
proposals.reason: 領、護 here are the Army Commander and Army Protector already defined in this chapter, not 'Colonel Directors/Protectors'.

proposals.before: Nightfall stranded the train past water-clock closing time—the royal coach shell stuck open until Wudi told Chen Xie to seal it.
proposals.after: The carriage turned back only when dusk pressed close; the clepsydra had run out, and the armored coach-box should have been closed; they halted the imperial carriage and long could not close it, so an edict ordered Xie to close it.
proposals.reason: Chinese has an edict 詔勰 without naming Wudi in this sentence; the idiomatic version invents Wudi as speaker.

proposals.before: 275 CE Yang Yao became household supervisor so tutors shed staff.
proposals.after: In 275 Yang Yao became household supervisor so the tutors shed their staff.
proposals.reason: 'CE Yang Yao' fuses the era abbreviation onto the personal name.

proposals.before: Wudi's heir's palace began with a central guard rate.
proposals.after: When Wudi built the Eastern Palace he established guard rates, first called the Central Guard Rate.
proposals.reason: The Chinese names Left and Right Guard Rates and states that Emperor Wu built the Eastern Palace and first called the office Central Guard Rate; the idiomatic sentence invents 'heir's palace' and drops the office name.

proposals.before: In the third year of Xianning Guards General Yang Yao and Palace Secretariat supervisor Xun Xu, fearing later troubles for Emperor Hui, cited former Minister of Works Pei Xiu's feudal plan and told Emperor Wu: "In antiquity establishing nobility was to screen and guard the royal house.
proposals.after: In the third year of Xianning, Guards General Yang Yao and Palace Secretariat supervisor Xun Xu, because Prince You of Qi enjoyed timely prestige and they feared later troubles for Emperor Hui, cited former Minister of Works Pei Xiu's five-grade feudal intent and calmly presented contemporary policy to Emperor Wu, saying: "In antiquity establishing nobility was to screen and guard the royal house.
proposals.reason: The idiomatic English omits 齊王攸有時望, fuses the year to the office title, and drops 從容共陳時宜.

proposals.before: Only Lu gained extra households; Shen and Yang Hu were bumped posthumously.
proposals.after: Only the Lu ducal fief had its households specially increased; former Minister of Works Duke of Boling Wang Shen was advanced to commandery duke, and Marquis of Juping Yang Hu to commandery marquis of Nancheng.
proposals.reason: Clipped 'Shen' obscures 王沈, and 追進封故司空 applies clearly to Wang Shen; the English also drops the specific titles.

proposals.before: Enforcement sent peers weeping from Luoyang.
proposals.after: Once implemented, those whose fiefs had been augmented were sent to their domains as originally memorialized, yet the dukes clung to the capital and departed weeping.
proposals.reason: The Chinese has 京師, not Luoyang; the idiomatic line invents the city name and omits 所增徙各如本奏遣就國.

decisions.reason: The Chinese is impersonal: Han terrace offices were abolished and Lord Cao then occupied the restored chancellorship; the original wrongly makes Cao Cao the agent of the abolition.
